newsitem.title: SPAIN: Iberian markets vulnerable to softer view of EMU.
newsitem.headline: Iberian markets vulnerable to softer view of EMU.

text.p: Iberian markets have turned vulnerable, as convergence towards Europe's single currency is now seen coming from a rise in core yields rather than a drop in rates in peripheral countries, analysts said on Thursday.

Two recent market shocks -- the surprise win of the left wing in the French first-round election vote and the Bundesbank-Bonn row over gold revaluation -- have drained the market of its former euphoria toward Europe's planned Economic and Monetary Union.

"Bonn's decision to go ahead with its plan seems to lead to a timely, softer and wider EMU. In principle this should not affect peripheral markets, but the convergence is more likely now via higher core yields than via peripherals falls," said Carlos Mazario economist at AFI in Madrid.
After an enthusiastic run toward EMU, the bono market suddenly realised that getting there wasn't the full story -- they also needed to know what the destination would look like once they arrived.
It was the Bundesbank late on Wednesday that jolted dealers and analysts into awareness.
In a harsh statement, the Bundesbank said it was disappointed at Bonn's plan to use gold revaluation in order to reduce its level of debt and help it meet euro launch criteria.
"The overall (EMU) project now has less credibility. And this is going to increase (market) volatility," said Kit Juckes, senior economist at Natwest in London.

A return to rollercoaster markets may be around the corner, as analysts see a higher possibility of a selloff in core markets given the new impression that the euro could be a softer currency than the mark.
"The effects are not clear for the spreads, but they are negative for debt markets, where the absolute value of long-term yields is set to rise," said Jose Luis Alzola at Salomon Brothers in London.
The Spanish 10-year spread over Bunds set its record low at 64 basis points one week ago versus 330 basis points on March 1996, with Portuguese bonds moving in a similar pattern.
But on Tuesday, markets fell with both the Bank of Spain and the Bank of Portugal forced to intervene and support their respective currencies.
The peseta, which was trading comfortably below the level of 84.50 per mark, closed yesterday at 84.87/90 per mark.
"The peseta is suffering from the uncertainty until the situation in Francia and Germany becomes clear," said Cesar Cantalapiedra, analyst at AFI in Madrid.
The long-bond future also suffered. The June contract was trading this morning at around 114.77, 22 basis points lower than yesterday. On Tuesday it was trading above 115.50.
The German government decision to use the gold revaluation to reduce its debt level could prompt the Bundesbank to raise its official rates sooner than previously expected, Alzola added.
"They may have to compensate for the inflationary impact of a possible increase in the money supply (from the revaluation)," he explained.
And Spanish shares, which have made a string of record highs this year, took the cue for a wave of profit taking. This morning the blue-chip Ibex-35 index was down 1.43 percent to 6,429 points.
The uncertain outlook could prove dangerous for stocks, analyst added.
"If it's bad for bonds it will in the end be bad for stocks," Alzola said.
One danger for markets is that the overall EMU project seems to have been flung back into public debate.
"The vote in France and the Buba-Bonn fight made clear that we need a more serious debate with people," said Valentin Fernandez, economist with Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
"There is a discrepancy between what markets and politicians were saying and what people thought," he added.
